content.user_title: Build Go Dependency Graphs with Google Wire
content.value_statement: Go dependency graphs become difficult to maintain as constructors and interfaces change. This skill guides Wire provider design, injector generation, cleanup handling, and testing.
actual_capabilities: Guide provider and injector definitions using wire.NewSet, wire.Build, and wireinject build constraints.
Explain explicit interface bindings and distinct named types for duplicate provider outputs.
Describe struct injection, field extraction, constant values, and prebuilt injector arguments.
Show cleanup provider signatures, reverse cleanup ordering, and partial construction failure handling.
Provide application wiring recipes for HTTP services, command-line applications, and separate development configurations.
Guide test doubles, test provider sets, and CI checks for generated source changes.
limitations: Requires Go and the Google Wire generator; the skill does not bundle these tools.
Google Wire is archived; assess maintenance and compatibility before adopting it for new projects.
Wire does not provide runtime containers, lifecycle hooks, or automatic signal handling.
Examples require project-specific types, dependencies, and validation; this audit did not execute them.

use_cases.title: Add compile-time application wiring
use_cases.description: Organize database, cache, repository, and service constructors into reusable provider sets with a generated application injector.

use_cases.title: Maintain generated dependency graphs
use_cases.description: Plan regeneration and CI checks after constructor changes, and keep generated source synchronized with provider definitions.

use_cases.title: Replace dependencies in integration tests
use_cases.description: Design test provider sets and explicit interface bindings that replace production dependencies with controlled fakes.

prompt_templates.title: Understand a basic Wire injector
prompt_templates.prompt: Explain how Google Wire connects these constructors: [constructor signatures]. Show the provider set, injector build constraint, and generation workflow.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner: introduce compile-time dependency injection into a small Go application.

prompt_templates.title: Fix a provider resolution error
prompt_templates.prompt: Diagnose this Wire error: [error]. Review these providers and interfaces: [code]. Explain the smallest binding or named-type change needed.
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate: resolve missing interface providers or duplicate output types.

prompt_templates.title: Design cleanup-aware application wiring
prompt_templates.prompt: Design Wire provider sets for [application components]. Include cleanup signatures, partial failure handling, prebuilt configuration arguments, and the caller's shutdown responsibilities.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: coordinate resource construction and cleanup across application packages.

prompt_templates.title: Plan test wiring and CI verification
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this Wire layout: [provider sets and injectors]. Plan fake interface bindings, test generation, and CI freshness checks. Identify build-tag and lifecycle risks.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: maintain separate production and test graphs with reproducible generated output.

output_examples.input: Wire generates my injector, but go build reports that InitApp is declared twice.
output_examples.output: The injector stub needs the wireinject build constraint. Exclude the stub from normal builds, regenerate the injector, and build again.

output_examples.input: Both database connection providers return strings, and Wire reports multiple bindings.
output_examples.output: Use distinct named types for primary and replica connection strings. Update the providers and database constructors so each dependency has a unique type.

output_examples.input: How can my integration tests replace the production mailer without changing production wiring?
output_examples.output: Create a test provider set that binds the mailer interface to a recording fake. Compose the test graph without the conflicting production mailer binding.

best_practices: Regenerate and review Wire output after constructor changes, then commit generated source with the provider changes.
Keep provider sets small and bind interfaces explicitly near their concrete providers.
Propagate cleanup functions through injectors and handle construction errors before scheduling cleanup.
anti_patterns: Editing generated injector bodies instead of changing providers and regenerating.
Providing multiple values of the same type without distinct named types.
Treating Wire as a runtime lifecycle framework with automatic startup and shutdown hooks.

faq.question: What does Google Wire generate?
faq.answer: Wire generates ordinary Go constructor calls from provider sets and injector declarations. The resulting application does not need a runtime dependency container.

faq.question: Does this skill install Go or Wire?
faq.answer: No tools are bundled. The instructions include installation commands, which require network access and permission to modify the development environment.

faq.question: Should I edit wire_gen.go to fix constructor errors?
faq.answer: No. Update the providers or injector declarations, regenerate the output, and review the changes.

faq.question: How are interfaces connected to implementations?
faq.answer: Use explicit wire.Bind declarations when providers return concrete implementations. Keep the concrete provider available in the relevant set.

faq.question: Does Wire manage graceful shutdown?
faq.answer: Wire can compose provider cleanup functions. You must still implement lifecycle coordination, signal handling, and graceful server shutdown.

faq.question: Is Google Wire still maintained?
faq.answer: The included documentation identifies Google Wire as archived. Verify current upstream status and Go compatibility before selecting it for a new project.
